subject: Science
chapter: Chapter 8: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
central_question: How can matter be classified as mixtures or pure substances, and how do elements and compounds differ in composition, properties, separation and use?
in_scope_units: Mixtures, components, uniform and non-uniform mixtures, alloys and air.
Evidence for carbon dioxide and dust in air and the distinction between components and pollutants.
Types of mixtures and the scientific meaning of a pure substance.
Decomposition of water and the definition and classification of elements.
Compounds, fixed ratios, new properties and physical versus chemical separation.
Sugar decomposition and comparison of iron–sulfur mixture with iron sulfide.
Uses of elements, compounds and mixtures, including advanced materials and minerals.

known_pitfalls.claim: A uniform mixture is automatically a pure substance.
known_pitfalls.correction: A uniform mixture still contains more than one pure component, even though the components are evenly distributed.

known_pitfalls.claim: The word pure has exactly the same meaning in daily life and science.
known_pitfalls.correction: In science, a pure substance contains only one type of particle and cannot be separated physically; an unadulterated food may still be a mixture.

known_pitfalls.claim: Compounds retain all the properties of their constituent elements.
known_pitfalls.correction: A compound has new properties different from those of the elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

known_pitfalls.claim: Iron and sulfur in Sample A cannot be separated.
known_pitfalls.correction: They retain their properties, and the iron can be removed with a magnet.

known_pitfalls.claim: Iron sulfide in Sample B is just a uniform mixture.
known_pitfalls.correction: Heating creates a new compound whose properties differ and whose elements cannot be separated physically.

recommended_example_progression: Use Activities 8.1 and 8.2 to identify carbon dioxide and dust in air.
Use Activity 8.3 to infer that water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
Use Activity 8.4 to infer that sugar contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Use Activity 8.5 to compare a mixture with the compound iron sulfide.
Use Keep the curiosity alive Q6 and Q7 for classification and word equations.
Use Q12 to connect gold with both the mineral and element categories.
